analysis.one_liner: Bans federal permits for sulfide mines within five miles of the Great Lakes unless operators prove no acid drainage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee at the end of the 109th Congress with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Sulfide mining, which pulls copper and nickel out of rock, can produce acid mine drainage — acidic, metal-laden water that leaks from mines and poisons rivers and lakes for decades. The bill would have barred any federal permit for a sulfide mine within five miles of a Great Lake unless the mining company could prove its operation would cause zero acid drainage into the Lakes. It was referred to committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 30 million people who live in the Great Lakes basin and drink, fish, and recreate in those waters, plus the tourism and fishing economies that depend on clean water. Preventing acid mine drainage matters because, once it starts, it is essentially impossible to stop and can keep polluting for centuries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Great Lakes basin residents and water users

how_it_helps.text: The bill placed the burden on mining companies: no federal permit for a sulfide mine within five miles of a Great Lake unless the applicant demonstrated there would be no acid mine drainage into the Lakes [S2][S3].
It spelled out its purpose as protecting Great Lakes water quality from the harmful effects of acid mine drainage [S3].
The five-mile buffer used the federal Clean Water Act definition of the Great Lakes, tying the protection to the lakes' existing legal boundary [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies seeking to open copper or nickel mines near the Great Lakes would bear the cost of proving zero acid drainage — a bar many could not meet — and could lose access to ore bodies near the lakes. Taxpayers could otherwise bear cleanup costs, since acid drainage from mines often persists after a mine closes.

drawbacks.text: The zero-drainage standard is close to impossible to satisfy, so critics would call it a de facto mining ban near the lakes rather than a safety standard; a company could argue the law forecloses even well-designed mines [S2][S3].
A five-mile buffer addresses only the lakes themselves; sulfide mines farther inland could still send acid drainage into the streams and groundwater that feed the Great Lakes [S3].
Restricting domestic mining near the lakes could push copper and nickel sourcing overseas, where environmental oversight may be weaker than at a carefully regulated U.S. site.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection it offered — keeping acid mine drainage out of 20 percent of the world's fresh surface water — far outweighed its costs for ordinary people, since acid drainage is effectively irreversible and cleanup falls on the public. The honest counterargument is that a flat five-mile, zero-drainage rule is blunt: it bans all nearby mining regardless of site quality, and it does nothing for mines just outside the buffer. A narrower standard tied to demonstrated containment might have protected the water while preserving some mining.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to a water subcommittee, and sat there until the 109th Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak of Michigan introduced the bill on March 9, 2006 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day [S1][S5].
Five days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, the last action ever taken on it [S1][S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill received no committee hearing, no floor vote, and no Senate companion before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies interested in sulfide deposits near the Great Lakes are better off: with the bill dead, no federal law forced them to prove zero acid drainage before getting a permit. The general public gained nothing from the bill's death, and the Great Lakes remain protected only by whatever permitting rules exist outside this proposal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining companies; the lakes got no new protection

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; his northern Michigan district sits on the Great Lakes shoreline, where sulfide mining was a live issue.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, passed it to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opponent is on the record; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan shape can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have made it far harder to win a federal permit for a sulfide mine within five miles of the Great Lakes, by requiring proof that the mine would cause zero acid drainage — a standard that in practice blocks most such mines. Its death left the permitting path open. The cost of acid drainage that does occur — fouled drinking water, dead streams, perpetual treatment — falls on nearby residents and taxpayers, not the mine's balance sheet.

industries.industry: Great Lakes fishing and tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses depend on clean lake water; a single acid drainage event near a Great Lake could damage fisheries and shore tourism for years. The bill's failure left them with the same exposure to mining proposals they had before.
